explanations.explanation: This neuron is essentially a “garbage‐character” detector: it spikes on stray replacement glyphs and garbled/HTML-entity residues (the “�” tokens and related weird encoding artifacts) that signal mis-decoded or malformed text.

This neuron is a “script‐switch” detector that spikes whenever the model sees non-Latin‐alphabet tokens (Hangul, Chinese characters, Arabic, Devanagari, Tamil, Thai, Katakana/Kanji, Bengali, etc.). It flags chunks of text written in any of those foreign scripts.

This feature fires on the “boilerplate” metadata tokens you see in sidebars, bylines and tables—date‐time stamps, author or “Published by…” lines, headings like “Description >,” weather or yield stats (percentages, degrees), distances, phone numbers, etc. In short, it marks tokens that carry structured page metadata rather than running prose.
This feature fires on “.” tokens whenever they serve as full-stop or abbreviation dots (e.g. sentence-final periods and the “.” in date or name abbreviations like “Oct.,” “D.C.,” “Sept.,” etc.).

This head appears to be a generic “script-switch” detector: it fires strongly on the tokens that mark the onset (and often the closing) of a span of non-Latin text (Korean, Japanese, Arabic, Devanagari, Cyrillic, etc.), especially at language-boundary points or when proper-noun/brand-name segments in those scripts begin or end.

The feature is a “trailing‐dot” detector—it lights up on the period that ends an uppercase or title-case abbreviation/initialism in headlines, names, dates, state codes or episode labels (e.g. “Nov.,” “K.,” “M.,” “WY.,” “Ep.”, etc.), effectively marking that structured punctuation boundary.
This neuron is a detector for the cardinal “one” used as a singular quantifier—especially in “one of…” or “one”-as-an-instance constructions that pick out a single example from a set.
This feature fires on title‐ or heading‐style phrases (title‐case word sequences at the start of a block), marking the end of a section header or document title.

This neuron flags small, highly emphasized “labels” or headings that kick off a new section or list item—often rendered in bold or as a stray non-Latin token (step numbers, foreign-script words, brand names, bullet markers, etc.) just before the main content.
This neuron flags tokens that include an internal period—i.e. abbreviations, initials, date or version markers, and decimal numbers (e.g. “U.S.C.”, “D.C.”, “Nov.”, “6.0”, “3.0.11”).

This feature fires on the “dot” in abbreviations and initialisms (e.g. month-abbrev “Oct.”, name initials “D.”, org-suffix “Inc.”, “U.S.”, “N.J.”, etc.)—i.e. the non-sentence-ending period that marks an abbreviation.

This feature fires on the final full‐stop of standalone, all‐caps headings or titles (e.g. press-release headlines, legal or terms-of-service banners, ad/service pitches, section labels), marking the end of a formatted header line.

This feature fires whenever the model encounters spans of non‐Latin, non‐ASCII script characters (e.g. Hangul, CJK ideographs, Arabic, Devanagari, etc.), signaling a switch into a foreign writing system.

This neuron fires on the “.” token when it’s being used as an abbreviation/initialism marker (e.g. “D.” in a name, “Inc.” in a company, “Jan.”/“Sept.” in dates, “Art.”/“Sec.” in legal citations, decimal points, “etc.”, etc.), distinguishing those internal‐sentence periods from ordinary full-stop punctuation.
This head is a “list/coordination” detector: it lights up on the small function words (and, or, of, etc.) that glue together items or phrases in enumerations, partitives, and coordinate structures.
This neuron fires on the little bracket-style markers that surround inline reference numbers or dates (e.g. the “[” and “]” around a year or citation index) in structured/Wikipedia‐like text.

This neuron fires on the “dot” punctuation when it serves as an internal separator—e.g. in decimal numbers (2.5, 5.7), abbreviations or initials (U.S., S.A., A.), date abbreviations (Aug., Sept.), and domain names or URLs (youtube.com, idf.org).

1. Recognizes the “Show posts in this category” footer on Japanese category pages.  
2. Marks the “Labels:” header followed by a list of taxonomy or tag names.  
3. Fires on bullet-point hotel policy sections detailing age-based charges (infant/child rates).  
4. Identifies user review/testimonial sections prompting visitors to read or leave recommendations.  
5. Tags Spanish devotional prose explaining how to pray in one’s own words.  
6. Captures social-media–style thank-you/event announcement posts (e.g. “Thanks everyone… See ya at…”).  
7. Appears in news-style reports of alleged misconduct or misbehavior in a personal dispute.  
8. Marks motivational blog intros using rhetorical questions about someone who “inspires” you.  
9. Triggers on DIY/home-improvement Q&A lines about cost per foot for fences.  
10. Fires on Korean corporate-registration or business-entity statements with numbers and “Ltd.”  
11. Detects management-consulting jargon about high-performance organizations and visionary leadership.  
12. Flags real-estate marketing pitches offering zero-down or “try before you buy” financing.  
13. Marks Korean/English technical product descriptions for database-historian or RDB tools.  
14. Captures Discuz-style forum metadata displays (user counts, recent posts, “Powered by Discuz”).  
15. Identifies article-listing headers that show a date and number of posts (e.g. “Showing 36 articles from August 6, 2014”).  
16. Fires on Arabic hotel renovation or rating announcements mentioning star-class and distance info.  
17. Marks German legal disclaimers and form-submission instructions for membership cards.  
18. Recognizes Persian bibliographic author listings (names with birth years or identifiers).  
19. Tags Korean content-release announcements referencing a title/brand (e.g. “Marange”) and episode numbers.  
20. Captures Chinese bibliographic reference entries with publication years, publishers, and ISBNs.
This neuron lights up on subword pieces that begin multi-piece capitalized strings—i.e. the initial token of a proper name, brand, acronym or CamelCase word.

This neuron fires on the hallmarks of marketing‐style copy – the “you/we” calls to action, modal verbs (“can/may/should”), to-infinitives, promotional adjectives (smart, wholesome, celebratory, etc.) and product or brand names/titles that typically appear in sales pitches or headings.
